The proof was to be brought the next day, before delay could cool our sense of honour. The next day Drummle arrived with a short, polite note in Estella’s handwriting, saying that she had had the honour of dancing with him several times. All I could do was regret that I had been ‘carried away by a heat of feeling which,’ and generally withdraw my challenge to meet him anywhere. Drummle and I then spent an hour snorting at each other, while everyone in the Grove contradicted everyone else. At last it was announced that friendly feeling had advanced at a remarkable pace.

I make light of this now, but it was far from light to me. I cannot fully describe how painful it was to think that Estella could favour such a worthless, awkward, sulky fool, so far below an ordinary man. Even now, I believe there was something truly generous and unselfish in my love for her that made the thought of her lowering herself to that brute unbearable. Certainly I would have been miserable whoever she had favoured. But a more deserving man would have hurt me in a different way, and not so deeply.

It was easy to discover, and I soon did discover, that Drummle had begun to pursue her closely, and that she let him. Before long, he was constantly following her, and he and I met every day. He persisted in his dull way, and Estella kept him going. Sometimes she encouraged him, sometimes discouraged him; sometimes she nearly flattered him, sometimes openly despised him; sometimes she knew him very well, sometimes she could scarcely remember who he was.

But the Spider, as Mr. Jaggers had named him, was accustomed to waiting for his chance and had all a spider’s patience. Besides that, he had a fool’s confidence in his money and his grand family. This sometimes served him well, almost doing the work of clear attention and firm purpose. So the Spider kept his stubborn watch on Estella, outlasting many cleverer insects, and often unfolded himself and dropped down at just the right moment.

At a public ball in Richmond—most places held such balls in those days—Estella had outshone every other beautiful woman. The blundering Drummle stayed so close to her, and she allowed it so readily, that I decided to speak to her about him. I took the next chance that came. She was sitting apart among some flowers, dressed and ready to leave, waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home.

I went next from one shop to another, buying what was needed to alter his appearance. Having completed this business, I made my way, on my own behalf, to Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers sat at his desk, but on seeing me come in he rose at once and placed himself before the fire.

‘Now, Pip,’ he said, ‘take care.’

‘I shall, sir,’ I answered. For on the way I had considered carefully what I meant to say.

‘Don’t compromise yourself,’ said Mr. Jaggers, ‘and don’t compromise anybody else. You understand—anybody. Tell me nothing: I have no wish to know anything; I have no curiosity.’

Naturally, I perceived that he knew the man had arrived.

‘All I wish, Mr. Jaggers,’ said I, ‘is to satisfy myself that what I have been told is true. I cannot hope it is false, but I can at least confirm it.’

Mr. Jaggers nodded. ‘But was your word “told” or “informed”?’ he inquired, inclining his head, and looking, not at me, but at the floor with an air of listening. ‘Told appears to suggest spoken communication. One cannot have spoken communication with a man in New South Wales, you know.’

‘Then I shall say informed, Mr. Jaggers.’

‘Good.’

‘I have been informed by someone called Abel Magwitch that he is the benefactor whose name was so long concealed from me.’

‘That is the man,’ said Mr. Jaggers, ‘in New South Wales.’

‘And nobody else?’ I asked.

‘And nobody else,’ said Mr. Jaggers.

‘I am not unreasonable enough, sir, to hold you responsible in any degree for my errors and mistaken conclusions; but I had always believed it was Miss Havisham.’

‘As you observe, Pip,’ replied Mr. Jaggers, fixing his eyes coolly on me and biting his forefinger, ‘I bear no responsibility for that.’

‘Yet it seemed so much like it, sir,’ I urged, heavy at heart.

‘Not a scrap of evidence, Pip,’ said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and drawing together his coat-skirts. ‘Accept nothing upon appearances; accept everything upon evidence. No rule is better.’

‘There is nothing more for me to say,’ I sighed, after a short silence. ‘My information has been confirmed, and that ends it.’

‘And now that Magwitch—in New South Wales—has finally revealed himself,’ said Mr. Jaggers, ‘you will appreciate, Pip, how strictly, in all my dealings with you, I have kept to the exact line of fact. There has never been the smallest deviation from that exact line of fact. You understand that fully?’

‘Fully, sir.’

‘I conveyed to Magwitch—in New South Wales—when he first addressed me—from New South Wales—the warning that he must never expect me to depart from the exact line of fact.

‘Why, surely you don’t mean—’ my sister began.

‘Indeed I do, Mum,’ said Pumblechook; ‘but have a little patience. Proceed, Joseph. Well done! Proceed!’

‘What would the company here say,’ Joe continued, ‘to twenty pound?’

‘Handsome is what I should call it,’ replied my sister.

‘Well, then,’ said Joe, ‘there’s more than twenty pound.’

That grovelling hypocrite, Pumblechook, nodded once more and remarked, with a condescending laugh, ‘More than that, Mum. Well done again! Keep her going, Joseph!’

‘Then to finish the matter,’ said Joe, joyfully placing the bag in my sister’s hands, ‘it’s five-and-twenty pound.’

‘Five-and-twenty pound, Mum,’ repeated that lowest of cheats, Pumblechook, getting up to shake her hand; ‘and no more than you deserve, as I remarked when my opinion was sought, and may the money bring you joy!’

Had the villain ended there, his offence would have been dreadful enough; but he deepened his guilt by next taking charge of me, claiming a patron’s authority that surpassed all his earlier criminal conduct.

‘Now observe, Joseph and wife,’ said Pumblechook, seizing my arm above the elbow, ‘I am a man who always carries through what he has started. This boy must be bound immediately. That is my manner of doing things. Bound immediately.’

‘Heaven knows, Uncle Pumblechook,’ said my sister, clutching the money, ‘how much we owe you.’

‘Don’t think of me, Mum,’ answered that fiendish cornchandler. ‘A pleasure is a pleasure wherever you go. But as for this boy, you know, we must get him bound. I promised I would attend to it—to speak plainly.’

The Justices were holding court at the neighbouring Town Hall, and we went there immediately to have me bound apprentice to Joe before the Magistrates. I call it going there, but Pumblechook pushed me there, precisely as though I had just robbed a pocket or set a hayrick alight. Indeed, the prevailing belief in Court was that I had been caught in the act; for while Pumblechook thrust me ahead of him through the crowd, I heard some ask, ‘What has he done?’ and others say, ‘A young one too, but don’t he look wicked?’ Someone with a gentle and charitable face actually presented me with a tract bearing a woodcut of an evil-looking young fellow furnished with a whole sausage-shop of chains, under the title TO BE READ IN MY CELL.

I thought the Hall a curious place, with pews taller than those in church—and people leaning over them to watch—and imposing Justices, one with a powdered head, reclining in chairs with their arms crossed, or taking snuff, or falling asleep, or writing, or reading newspapers—and glossy black portraits upon the walls, which to my untrained eye appeared made of hardbake and sticking-plaster.
